text:
Eni S.p.A. (NYSE:E) and Malaysia's national oil company, Petronas, have signed a feasibility agreement to explore the development of high-performance bio-gasoline for motorsport, with the possibility of eventually scaling the technology for commercial use. The partnership brings together Eni's Ecofining renewable fuel technology and Petronas' experience in developing high-performance racing fuels. Since the project is still at the feasibility stage, it is unlikely to have any meaningful impact on either company's near-term earnings or cash flow. For now, it should be viewed primarily as a strategic research and development opportunity.

Eni: Biofuel Ambitions Offer Long-Term Upside but Face Commercialization Risks

For Eni S.p.A. (NYSE:E), the partnership gives the company a relatively capital-efficient way to expand its sustainable mobility business beyond conventional HVO diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Through its Enilive subsidiary, Eni already has a sizeable biofuels infrastructure across Europe. Using motorsport, particularly Formula 1, as a testing ground could give Eni an opportunity to put bio-gasoline through demanding real-world conditions while limiting the risk to its existing commercial fuel operations. If the technology can eventually be produced at scale, Eni could use what it learns from the project to develop drop-in bio-gasoline for wider transportation markets, strengthening its broader strategy of using multiple technologies to support decarbonization.

The biggest issue for Eni S.p.A. (NYSE:E) is likely to be the time required to turn the project into a meaningful commercial business. A feasibility study does not guarantee that the technology will reach the market, and converting a specialized, expensive racing fuel into an affordable product for everyday consumers could prove challenging.

Fluctuating feedstock costs, regulatory requirements and the economics of large-scale production could all make commercialization more difficult. As a result, investors are unlikely to significantly change their view of Eni based on this announcement alone, particularly while the project remains focused on research and development.

Petronas: Sustainable Fuel Push Creates Strategic Potential Amid Uncertain Returns

For Petronas, the agreement offers a chance to tap into established biofuel technology without having to develop the entire processing chain on its own. As motorsport moves toward tighter emissions and carbon-reduction requirements, having access to dependable advanced sustainable fuels could become increasingly important for Petronas' racing activities. Working with Eni gives Petronas access to European expertise in biorefining and could help speed up its development of lower-carbon fuel products. At the same time, the project could strengthen Petronas' reputation in alternative energy and sustainable fuel technologies.

The Energy Ministry publishes a strategic plan for Israel’s fuel economy through 2040 that includes moving the Bazan oil refineries from the northern city of Haifa to the south of the country, contrary to a 2022 government decision to close them down and end domestic refining.

Conducted by the BDO consulting firm, the study emphasizes that relying solely on imported refined products poses excessive national security risks during wartime or global crises.

The proposed “clear-and-build” initiative, estimated to cost $5 to $6 billion, would involve establishing a hybrid refinery in southern Israel that could eventually also make products such as sustainable aviation fuel and biodiesel.

Rather than compensating Bazan for closure, the plan suggests using state revenues from carbon taxes to move the facility.

The plan also includes expanding emergency fuel stores, upgrading port and storage infrastructure, and establishing additional fuel entry points.

An inter-ministerial team will examine creating a dedicated fuel authority to oversee implementation of the plan.

text:
At a key leaders' summit in Palau, Pacific island nations burdened by worsening climate change impacts and costly fossil fuel imports called for November's COP31 climate summit to deliver finance to help the region transition to renewable energy and build more resilient communities.

Heads of government from the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) – which includes COP31 co-president Australia – met in Palau's capital Koror for a week-long summit, where they demanded access to climate finance, ocean action and a regional boost for renewables at COP31.

Palau's president Surangel Whipps Jr. said during a plenary session that the Pacific must focus on delivering climate and ocean commitments. "It will require greater regional leadership, stronger regional coordination and, above all, unity of purpose," he said.

The meeting, which ended last Friday, was marked by the absence of some leaders – among them the heads of state of the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and Fiji, which will host a preparatory session for COP31 in October (referred to as the pre-COP31). There were also tensions over Taiwan's participation, with China objecting to its presence as an observer.

The forum's final declaration, published after it ended and signed by all its members, reaffirms that climate change is the "single greatest threat to the security, livelihoods and wellbeing of Pacific peoples", and notes "the importance of a focused, high-level declaration" at the pre-COP31 to build "political momentum towards COP31".

Australia and Pacific islands have invited world leaders to attend the pre-COP31 gathering, which will be held in Fiji and Tuvalu from October 5 to 8. While usually a technical meeting for negotiators, the island nations aim to issue a political declaration at the gathering calling for strong outcomes in Türkiye.

Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said in a speech during the Pacific forum that his country is "determined to use COP31 to progress the agenda to make it easier for countries to access the climate finance they need".

"We won’t miss the opportunity to ensure COP31 is a Pacific COP. Not just because of the location of pre-COP but because of the agenda we are shaping through the Action Agenda at COP31," he said.

The Action Agenda is a large portfolio of climate initiatives and coalitions uniting governments, businesses and civil society outside of the formal negotiations on everything from health to methane emissions.

Renewable energy investment plan

Announced a year ago, the island nations launched a $14-billion investment plan for a "100% Renewable Blue Pacific" at the forum in Palau. The plan lists strategic projects that would reduce the region's high dependence on fossil fuel imports, whose soaring costs have become a major burden since the Iran war.

The projects include a $52-million programme managed by Australia to develop off-grid renewables in remote communities across the Pacific, as well as a $100-million blended finance fund aimed at supporting private-sector investments in wind and solar, among others.

Currently, some countries in the Pacific are spending up to a quarter of their GDP importing diesel to power electricity generation, according to a new report by the University of New South Wales in Australia. The investment plan launched at the forum aims to reduce these costs by adding 2.2 gigawatts of renewable generation and around 9 gigawatt hours of electricity storage.

To channel funds into the region, the plan also highlights the role of the recently established Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF), a regional fund that seeks to swiftly disburse funds to climate-vulnerable communities at the local level. Bowen said he would promote the facility to world leaders attending COP31 and "ask for their support".

Call to transition away from fossil fuels

Separately, the forum endorsed the Belau Declaration which emphasises the need to keep the 1.5C Paris Agreement temperature goal alive. A UN report last week showed that overshooting this limit is now inevitable, but deep emissions cuts could still bring global temperatures back down by the end of the century.

Pacific nations expect to rally support for this declaration at the pre-COP, with Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya saying in a statement: "Palau is where we build the political mandate. Pre-COP is where we take it to the world."

The political declaration also says that countries must accelerate the global transition away from fossil fuels "towards a renewable energy future", and calls for greater recognition of the importance of ocean health in addressing climate change.

UN sets out narrow path back to 1.5C warming after inevitable overshoot

As part of the forum's outcomes in Palau, countries also noted Tuvalu's efforts to host the second global conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, which will gather government representatives in April next year to follow up on this year's inaugural conference in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Speaking to journalists at the forum, Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu questioned Australia's role in talks about phasing out fossil fuels at COP31, adding that "the very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that". During the PIF, the country approved the extension of a major mine that digs and exports coal for steel-making, giving it permission to keep producing until 2055.

Rising seas trigger "development emergency"

As leaders met in one of the world's regions most threatened by sea-level rise, UN Secretary-General António Guterres released a new report warning that rising seas are now "one of the most profound threats to populations around the world in developed and developing states alike".

Presenting the report at UN headquarters in New York, Assistant Secretary-General for Economic Development Navid Hanif said rising sea levels are not a "future risk any more" but an accelerating "development emergency" that could hinder progress in vulnerable regions like the Pacific and least developed countries.

The report warns that seas are rising "faster than at any point in recorded history", with 2024 setting a new record of 5.9 millimetres. This has been driven by human-induced climate change mainly through a process known as thermal expansion – where rising heat causes the ocean to expand – as well as the melting of ice sheets.

Pacific islands seek backing for new regional fund ahead of COP31

The report notes that about 1.2 billion people around the world are exposed to coastal flooding, and says some low-lying islands in Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands and Fiji are already facing forced relocations. Globally, rising seas could cost more than $1 trillion every year by 2050, it adds.

"We cannot stop sea level rise this century but we can determine how much worse it becomes. About half a metre of sea level rise is already locked in in this century because of warming that has already occurred, but beyond that our choices matter enormously," Hanif told journalists.

Bill Hare, CEO of think-tank Climate Analytics, said the report was a "wake-up call" to the leaders of high-emitting countries that their failure to cut carbon emissions is "creating major risks for the future alongside the impacts we can already observe around us".

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from local waste biomass and has ambitions to construct four UK facilities to produce bioethanol for upgrading to SAF.
Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, such as wood chips, sawdust or wheat straw, into ethanol, which can be used to make SAF and renewable diesel.
Nova Pangaea is planning more trials next year to “fine tune” the design of the first commercial-scale plant, it said.

UK SAF developer Nova Pangaea Technologies reports it has successfully completed endurance trials at its Teesside demonstration plant to further validate its process of producing sustainable aviation fuel from waste biomass. The company says the trials, which used softwood residues from timber processing, showed continuous stable operation in production runs of up to 72 hours and achieved above target yields. Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from local waste biomass and has ambitions to construct four UK facilities to produce bioethanol for upgrading to SAF. Meanwhile, the UK Department for Transport, which has provided funding support for Speedbird, has released an updated comprehensive list of feedstocks, including wastes and residues, eligible under its SAF Mandate.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, such as wood chips, sawdust or wheat straw, into ethanol, which can be used to make SAF and renewable diesel. It also produces a biochar co-product, which can permanently capture carbon to make the whole process carbon negative by removing more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases, explains the company.

In the latest trials, multiple runs were carried out processing up to three tonnes of feedstock per day. They follow initial smaller-scale trials in early 2025 that demonstrated the viability of the process outside of the laboratory. Nova Pangaea is planning more trials next year to “fine tune” the design of the first commercial-scale plant, it said.

“The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building this first commercial plant,” commented, Stewart Stewart of Nova Pangaea, who joined the company as CEO earlier this year from New York-based investment bank Javelin Capital, where he advised on green fuel opportunities.

The company says it has raised over £21 million ($28m) to date from investors that include International Airlines Group, PXN Ventures, Mercia Ventures and the first Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund, as well as the government’s grant funding awarded under the Advanced Fuels Fund competition.

Added Stewart: “By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions.”

The Project Speedbird collaboration is expected to result in eventual production of 90,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel annually, with the potential, claims Nova Pangaea, to reduce net CO2 emissions by up to 541,800 tonnes a year on a lifecycle basis. British Airways is a founding investor and shareholder in US SAF producer LanzaJet, whose alcohol-to-jet technology that converts second-generation ethanol from sources like agricultural residues and woody biomass will be used in Project Speedbird.

Meanwhile, the Department of Transport has released an updated list of feedstocks, including wastes and residues, eligible under the UK’s SAF Mandate. The list, divided into categories, includes names and descriptions of the materials.

text:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel (RD) project developer Jet Zero Australia announced today that it has raised $30 million in a new funding round, with proceeds from the financing aimed at advancing the company’s Project Ulysses, a commercial-scale SAF and RD refinery in Townsville, Australia.

Founded in 2021 North Queensland by Ed Mason, Jet Zero develops and operates sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel projects, focusing on developing a biofuels production capacity in regional Australia.

The company said that the new capital will primarily fund completion of Front-End Engineering Design and support the project’s continued advancement towards Final Investment Decision and construction.

The funding round received backing from institutional investors including Qantas and Airbus, both of which had initially invested in Jet Zero in 2023. Jet Zero also announced that South Korean global trading and energy company Posco International will join the company as a strategic investor, with the companies exploring opportunities across fuel offtake, infrastructure and feedstock, subject to further agreement.

Ed Mason, Jet Zero Australia Chief Executive Officer, said:

“Completing our $30 million funding round, welcoming POSCO INTERNATIONAL and securing final development approval are defining milestones for Project Ulysses… Some organisations will buy low carbon liquid fuels. Others will invest in building the industry. We are fortunate to be backed by organisations committed to doing both.”

Jet Zero said that the new project has received its final Development Permit Decision Notice from the Queensland Office of the Coordinator-General, completing its principal development approvals.

According to the company, the project is expected to create approximately 1,000 jobs during construction and 100 permanent operational roles, while supporting the development of a broader Australian biofuels industry capable of supporting more than 18,000 jobs by 2040 across feedstock production, agriculture, refining, manufacturing and logistics.

Fiona Messent, Qantas Group Chief Sustainability Officer, said:

“Establishing domestic SAF production in Australia will support fuel security, create jobs and help aviation and Australia meet its decarbonisation objectives. Australia has the feedstock and the industry support to refine SAF here, and companies like Jet Zero can help put that to work.”

Neste (ISIN FI0009013296) stock is trading steadily as of September 7, 2026, with investors focusing on the company’s latest reported earnings and margins in its renewable fuels business amid an increasingly competitive global biofuels market.

Recent earnings frame Neste’s valuation

In that same recent reporting period, Neste’s renewable products segment showed a tangible improvement in profitability compared with the previous year, with higher sales volumes and an improved sales mix helping to lift segment operating profit. For investors, the key comparison is that segment operating profit in the latest quarter was higher than in the corresponding quarter a year earlier, reflecting both volume growth and margin support from market demand for low-carbon fuels.

Biofuel demand and feedstock costs shape expectations

Market data and sector commentary in early September 2026 highlight strong structural demand for biofuels, including renewable diesel and biodiesel blends, while also pointing to ongoing volatility in feedstock and fossil diesel prices as a backdrop for Neste’s earnings. In some markets, regulators and policymakers are preparing higher blend mandates for biodiesel and other renewable fuels toward 2027, which can support volume growth but also intensify competition for feedstocks such as used cooking oil, animal fats, and vegetable oils.

At the same time, recent reports on diesel price adjustments in various regions during September 2026 illustrate how fossil diesel benchmarks have moved higher in response to supply constraints and tax structures. This environment can make renewable diesel more cost-competitive over the lifecycle, but it also influences Neste’s margin outlook, because the company’s selling prices and spread versus fossil diesel are closely tied to broader energy market developments.

Renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel as growth pillars

Neste’s business model is built around renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, both produced from waste and residue feedstocks, and these products remain the core driver of long-term earnings. The most recent segment data from the company’s reporting show that renewable products account for a significant share of total revenue and an even larger share of operating profit, reflecting higher margins than traditional oil products. text:
Cathay Pacific and Google trial AI technology to cut climate impact of aircraft trails

Google and Cathay Pacific have partnered to test AI-powered technology that could help airlines avoid conditions that lead to persistent aircraft contrails, which can contribute to atmospheric warming. The trial is being conducted across Cathay Pacific's flight network, with a second phase now planned to collect more operational data. Cathay Pacific is Google's first commercial airline partner in Asia-Pacific to trial the contrail mitigation technology and the first airline globally to test the system on ultra-long-haul flights.

How the AI system identifies contrail-forming areas

Google's system combines AI-based predictive models, satellite imagery and weather data to forecast areas where aircraft are likely to form contrails. Flight dispatchers and pilots can use the forecasts to adjust an aircraft's altitude and route to avoid those areas. Cathay Pacific integrates the forecasts into its Electronic Flight Folder, alongside real-time operational information, allowing pilots to access the data in the cockpit.

What are aircraft contrails

Contrails are thin clouds that can form behind aircraft when they fly through cold and humid conditions at high altitude. While many disappear quickly, some can persist and spread into larger cloud formations that trap heat in the atmosphere. The companies cited previous research suggesting that persistent contrails could account for around one-third of aviation's total climate impact, making them an area of research alongside carbon dioxide emissions.

Trial covered more than 100 flights

The initial operational trial began in late 2025 and targeted more than 100 flights across Cathay Pacific's network. More than 80 flights ultimately followed contrail-avoidance routes. Google estimates that those flights achieved about a 40% reduction in the warming impact of contrails. The release notes that not all of the targeted flights participated because of factors including airspace and payload restrictions. The Hong Kong-Singapore corridor was among the routes tested. Early analysis found that relatively small altitude adjustments could prevent contrail formation, with actions on that route accounting for more than half of the trial's total climate impact.

Second phase will expand flight trials

Google and Cathay Pacific are now starting a larger second phase of trials across Cathay's Asia and transpacific network. The partners said the additional flights will provide more real-world operational data to assess contrail avoidance and its potential climate benefits. Nonprofit initiative Contrails.org is also participating in the project. The companies said more research is needed to determine how contrail avoidance could work across different airlines and airspaces. The resulting data could also contribute to future industry practices and policy discussions.

Cathay Pacific continues to focus on carbon dioxide emissions

Cathay Pacific said reducing carbon dioxide emissions remains a primary focus through measures including fleet modernisation, operational efficiency improvements and the use of sustainable aviation fuel. The partnership with Google is focused on the separate issue of non-CO₂ climate effects, including contrails.
